metadata.description: Clients reach two API replicas through a load balancer. The API uses Redis cache-aside: it looks each read up in Redis and, on a miss, reads PostgreSQL itself and writes the value back. Writes go to PostgreSQL and then invalidate the cached key. metadata.description: Checkout on Kubernetes with HPA autoscaling behind a Kong gateway, PostgreSQL with two read replicas, a Redis catalog cache and a third-party payments API. The API uses Redis cache-aside: it looks catalog reads up in Redis and, on a miss or if Redis fails, reads PostgreSQL itself. Checkouts write the order and then charge the card. Traffic ramps from 300 to 1,500 req/s: watch the pods fall behind the ramp until the autoscaler catches up, and payments dominate the tail. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.
metadata.name: Black Friday on Kubernetes

output.title: Checkout API is the primary bottleneck
output.detail: On average 88% of its 48 workers were busy, peaking at 100%. The queue averaged 107.9 requests (peak 300) and kept growing. 311 requests (17.8%) were rejected (queue full: 311). At the observed 61.8 ms per request it can sustain about 777 req/s; it received 954 req/s. Only 17% of busy worker time was its own processing; the rest was spent blocked on downstream calls.
output.suggestion: Add replicas or workers per replica, or reduce the service time. Faster dependencies (or non-blocking I/O) would also free workers.

output.title: Only 598 of 955 req/s completed successfully
output.detail: Success rate 82.1%; 313 requests failed and 0 timed out in the measurement window.

output.title: Main cause of failed requests
output.detail: 313 requests failed at Checkout API: queue was full (100% of all failures).

output.title: Catalog cache hit ratio 84%
output.detail: 84% of reads were served from the cache; 76 reads/s missed and Checkout API read them from Orders DB.

output.title: Orders DB read replicas served 67% of reads
output.detail: 2 replicas per shard took 93 of 139 reads; all 241 writes still went to the primary.
output.suggestion: Writes are most of the load, so replicas add little: shard the data or make writes cheaper.

output.title: Payments API failed 1.2% of calls
output.detail: 3 of 244 calls (1.2%) failed with provider errors; none reached the clients.
output.suggestion: Retry idempotent calls with exponential backoff and jitter (max attempts on the link), set a timeout, and add a fallback or circuit breaker so provider errors do not fail whole requests.

output.title: Checkout API autoscaled from 2 to 14 replicas
output.detail: The first new replica was taking traffic by about 0.1 s and capacity reached 14 replicas by about 1.2 s. 10 requests were rejected while it scaled. It scaled back to 13 replicas when load dropped.
output.suggestion: Scale earlier (lower target utilization or a shorter evaluation interval), keep more minimum replicas, or reduce start-up time.

output.title: Checkout API hit its autoscaling maximum (14 replicas)
output.detail: It ran at 88% utilization with no room left to scale.
output.suggestion: Raise max replicas (and check the database and other dependencies can take the extra load).

metadata.description: A user-profile service. A mobile app (65% of requests, one retry) and a web app (35%) call a Go profile API on four instances behind a load balancer. MySQL 8 runs a primary for writes and three read replicas that serve every read; each replica applies the primary's changes on 4 worker threads (replica_parallel_workers, MySQL 8's default), at about 70% of the original write's time. 1,500 req/s over 200,000 users, 10% of them profile and settings updates. Replication is asynchronous, so the request path says little here: a replica can fall seconds behind while every request succeeds, and a replica read of a profile whose latest change it has not applied yet is stale. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.
metadata.name: User profiles on MySQL: replica lag and stale reads

output.title: No component is saturated
output.detail: The busiest component is Profiles (MySQL 8) at 11% utilization. Throughput tracks the offered load.

output.title: Profiles (MySQL 8) read replicas served 13% of reads
output.detail: 3 replicas per shard took 300 of 2,269 reads; all 254 writes still went to the primary.
output.suggestion: Replica reads can be stale while replicas replay the primary's writes (see replication lag).

output.title: Profiles (MySQL 8) replicas lag up to 2.5 s behind the primary
output.detail: Replicas replay the primary's writes; they fell up to 2.5 s behind. 254 writes in the window had to be replayed, and 12 of 300 replica reads returned stale data.
output.suggestion: Writes outpace replay. Make writes cheaper, shard the writes, use a database with parallel replay (or raise replica apply workers), or read your own writes from the primary.

metadata.description: A Java API (Redis cache-aside in front of PostgreSQL) on a Kubernetes cluster with the horizontal pod autoscaler and the cluster autoscaler. A spike makes the HPA ask for more pods within seconds, but the two nodes are full: new pods wait as Pending until a node is provisioned (about 2 minutes), pull their image and start. Until then the pods that fit queue and refuse requests.
metadata.name: Kubernetes spike: pods wait for nodes

output.title: Catalog API is the primary bottleneck
output.detail: On average 91% of its 48 workers were busy. The queue averaged 211.9 requests (peak 300) and kept growing. 712 requests (50.2%) were rejected (queue full: 173, queue timeout: 539). Its CPU cores can do about 142 req/s at 10.6 ms of work per request; it received 371 req/s.
output.suggestion: Give it more CPU cores (or more replicas/instances), or reduce the CPU work per request.

output.title: Only 138 of 371 req/s completed successfully
output.detail: Success rate 47.3%; 748 requests failed and 0 timed out in the measurement window.

output.title: Main cause of failed requests
output.detail: 575 requests failed at Catalog API: waited longer than the queue timeout (77% of all failures).

breakdown.reasonText: waited longer than the queue timeout

output.title: Product cache hit ratio 89%
output.detail: 89% of reads were served from the cache; 13 reads/s missed and Catalog API read them from Products DB.

output.title: Products DB read replicas served 67% of reads
output.detail: 2 replicas per shard took 34 of 51 reads; all 59 writes still went to the primary.
output.suggestion: Writes are most of the load, so replicas add little: shard the data or make writes cheaper.

output.title: Pods waited up to 46 s for room on prod
output.detail: Up to 3 pod(s) waited for a node with room for their requests, the longest 46 s. The cluster autoscaler added 2 node(s), each ready about 120 s after it was asked for; 1 pod(s) were still Pending at the end.
output.suggestion: Keep headroom (more nodes, or a lower HPA target), use faster-provisioning nodes or smaller pod requests, or raise the maximum node count.

metadata.description: An orders API with three kinds of clients: a React web app (one attempt, 10 s timeout), a mobile app (two attempts) and partner integrations, which call through their own Kong gateway that enforces their plan's 450 req/s quota (their SDK makes three attempts with a 5 s timeout). Every new order is scored by a third-party fraud API, through an Envoy egress proxy, before it is committed to PostgreSQL; reads only touch PostgreSQL. The API is a Java service with a fixed thread pool, so a slow dependency holds threads that reads need too. The scenarios slow the fraud API 8× for 30 s and then add one defence at a time: fewer retries, a circuit breaker, failing open. The results show each client group separately. The fraud provider's fees are left out of the cost. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.

metadata.description: An accounts API (balances, orders, transfers) used by a mobile app (55% of traffic; one retry), a web app (30%) and partner integrations (15%; three attempts), behind a Kong gateway. Every request carries an OAuth access token. The Go API checks it with the identity provider's introspection endpoint, which allows 200 calls a second, and caches the answer in Redis for 60 s, keyed by token (cache-aside; the hit rate is worked out from the TTL and how often each of 5,000 active users calls). Writes that move money always ask the identity provider again (step-up), so a revoked token cannot move money; they carry an idempotency key, so clients may retry them. Traffic ramps from 150 to 1,350 req/s over the run. The scenarios take the cache away, shorten its TTL, take the identity provider down, and check JWTs locally for reads. The identity provider is usually priced per active user, so its fees are left out of the cost. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.
metadata.name: API auth: token introspection vs local JWT checks

The Go API checks it with the identity provider's introspection endpoint, which allows 200 calls a second, and caches the answer in Redis for 60 s, keyed by token (cache-aside; the hit rate is worked out from the TTL and how often each of 5,000 active users calls). Writes that move money always ask the identity provider again (step-up), so a revoked token cannot move money; they carry an idempotency key, so clients may retry them. Traffic ramps from 150 to 1,350 req/s over the run. The scenarios take the cache away, shorten its TTL, take the identity provider down, and check JWTs locally for reads. The identity provider is usually priced per active user, so its fees are left out of the cost. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.
metadata.name: API auth: token introspection vs local JWT checks

output.detail: Calls to Identity provider (introspection) take 100 ms on average, while the median request takes 164 ms end to end.
output.suggestion: If the user does not need the result right away, call it asynchronously through a queue; otherwise cache responses and keep its timeout well below the client's.

output.detail: 483 of 1,308 requests (36.9%) were turned away because they exceeded the rate limit of 200 req/s.
output.suggestion: Stay under the limit: queue or batch the calls, cache responses, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, or ask for a higher limit.

output.title: During the outage of Identity provider (introspection) (1.067-1.467 s) success fell from 100.0% to 65.3%
output.detail: Inside the fault window 65.3% of requests succeeded (before: 100.0%); p95 latency averaged 350 ms (before: 317 ms). It had not recovered by the time arrivals stopped. Identity provider (introspection) refused 286 calls while it was down; 87 client requests failed because of it.
output.suggestion: Add a fallback (or queue the work for later), with a timeout and a circuit breaker so the failure stays contained.

metadata.description: Clients reach two API replicas through a load balancer. The API uses Redis cache-aside: it looks each read up in Redis and, on a miss, reads PostgreSQL itself and writes the value back. Writes go to PostgreSQL and then invalidate the cached key. If Redis fails, reads fall back to PostgreSQL and invalidations are skipped. All performance numbers are illustrative assumptions, not measurements.

output.detail: Inside the fault window 80.0% of requests succeeded (before: 100.0%); p95 latency averaged 86 ms (before: 97 ms). It recovered as soon as the fault ended.
output.suggestion: Budget timeouts for the extra latency, retry on another instance, or cut the number of sequential calls across this link.

output.detail: Inside the fault window 80.0% of requests succeeded (before: 100.0%); p95 latency averaged 86 ms (before: 97 ms). It recovered as soon as the fault ended. PostgreSQL received no calls while it was down.
output.suggestion: Add a replica with automatic failover, and fail fast (timeouts, circuit breaker) so callers do not pile up while it is down.

output.title: During the outage of Redis Cache (1.5-2.5 s) success fell from 100.0% to 80.0%
output.detail: Inside the fault window 80.0% of requests succeeded (before: 100.0%); p95 latency averaged 86 ms (before: 97 ms). It recovered as soon as the fault ended. Redis Cache received no calls while it was down.
output.suggestion: Treat cache errors as misses and fall back to the database: turn on 'Carry on if this call fails' on the link to the cache and set the link to the database to 'Reads only on a cache miss' (check the database can take every read), or run a replicated cache.

output.title: During the outage of Load Balancer (1.5-2.5 s) success fell from 100.0% to 80.0%
output.detail: Inside the fault window 80.0% of requests succeeded (before: 100.0%); p95 latency averaged 86 ms (before: 97 ms). It recovered as soon as the fault ended. Load Balancer received no calls while it was down.
output.suggestion: Run redundant instances behind a load balancer and retry on another instance, so losing one component does not stop traffic.

metadata.description: A single service with 4 workers and exponential 10 ms service time (an M/M/4 queue, capacity 400 req/s). Compare the scenarios to see latency explode near saturation, and how a queue timeout sheds load instead of wasting work on requests whose clients already gave up.

metadata.description: A user-profile service. A mobile app (65% of requests, one retry) and a web app (35%) call a Go profile API on four instances behind a load balancer. MySQL 8 runs a primary for writes and three read replicas that serve every read; each replica applies the primary's changes on 4 worker threads (replica_parallel_workers, MySQL 8's default), at about 70% of the original write's time. 1,500 req/s over 200,000 users, 10% of them profile and settings updates. Replication is asynchronous, so the request path says little here: a replica can fall seconds behind while every request succeeds, and a replica read of a profile whose latest change it has not applied yet is stale. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.
metadata.name: User profiles on MySQL: replica lag and stale reads

output.title: No component is saturated
output.detail: The busiest component is Profiles (MySQL 8) at 11% utilization. Throughput tracks the offered load.

output.title: Profiles (MySQL 8) read replicas served 67% of reads
output.detail: 3 replicas per shard took 80 of 120 reads; all 400 writes still went to the primary.
output.suggestion: Writes are most of the load, so replicas add little: shard the data or make writes cheaper.
